stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Observational studies have long linked higher blood levels of vitamin D to fewer bone fractures, yet several large trials that gave vitamin D supplements to broad samples of adults found no reduction in fractures. Rather than conclude that the supplements are ineffective, nutrition scientist Priya Raman designed a new trial that enrolled only adults whose blood vitamin D fell below the deficiency threshold at the outset. Raman's design suggests that, in her view, ______
choices: vitamin D supplements cannot reduce fracture risk in adults whose blood levels are already above the deficiency threshold.
the link found in observational studies reflects other habits of adults with high vitamin D rather than the vitamin itself.
the earlier trials may have included too many adults who had little to gain from taking additional vitamin D.
the earlier trials demonstrated that supplements reduce fractures only in adults whose blood vitamin D was initially deficient.
explanation: Start with why Raman would run the trial this way. She refuses to read the earlier null results as proof that supplements fail, and she then enrols only deficient adults. That choice only makes sense if she thinks any benefit shows up mainly in deficient people, so a broad sample full of people who already had enough vitamin D could have hidden a real effect. Choice C states that belief. Its 'may' also fits the evidence: she is testing an explanation, not asserting one she has already proven.

A.why: You saw the key point, that the benefit is concentrated in deficient adults, and then took it one step too far. Raman's design only needs her to think adequate-level adults gain less, so including them would weaken the signal. It doesn't need her to think they gain nothing. 'Cannot' is strength creep.

B.why: You gave Raman a belief that her own action argues against. If she thought the observational link came from other habits and not from vitamin D, she would have no reason to run another supplement trial. The passage also says she specifically declined to conclude that the supplements are ineffective.

D.why: You turned Raman's hypothesis into a finding of the earlier trials. Those trials found no reduction in fractures, and nothing says they compared deficient and non-deficient adults. The idea that deficiency matters belongs to Raman's new design, not to their results.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Print historians have often ordered the undated impressions of a single etched plate by the sharpness of their lines: because each pass through the press wears the copper slightly, crisper impressions were assumed to be earlier. Studying the etchings of the nineteenth-century printmaker Odile Ferrant, historian Ana Kovač noted that Ferrant's workshop periodically re-bit worn plates in acid, deepening their lines. Kovač therefore set line sharpness aside and ordered Ferrant's impressions by the dated watermarks in their paper. Kovač's approach suggests that she regarded ______
choices: the dated watermarks as a less dependable guide than line sharpness to the order of Ferrant's impressions.
a crisp impression from one of Ferrant's plates as possibly later than a faint impression from that plate.
impressions pulled after one of Ferrant's plates was re-bitten as crisper than those pulled when it was new.
line sharpness as uninformative about the order of the impressions from any etched plate of the nineteenth century.
explanation: Ask why Kovač dropped line sharpness. The old method depends on lines only ever getting fainter over time. Re-biting deepens worn lines, so an impression pulled after re-biting can look crisp even though it came late. For that reason Kovač can't trust 'crisper means earlier' for Ferrant's plates, which means she must accept that a crisp impression might come after a faint one. Choice B says exactly that, and 'possibly' keeps it as strong as the passage allows and no stronger.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. Kovač gave up line sharpness and used watermarks instead, so she must think watermarks are the more dependable guide for Ferrant's work, not the less dependable one.

C.why: You understood that re-biting restores crispness, then added a step the passage never takes. 'Deepening their lines' only means re-bitten plates are crisper than they were when worn. Nothing says they become crisper than the plate was when new, and Kovač's method doesn't depend on that comparison.

D.why: You stretched one workshop's practice into a rule about every plate. Kovač's reason for dropping line sharpness is specific to Ferrant, whose workshop re-bit its plates. Her approach says nothing about plates that were never re-bitten, and 'any' goes well past what she needs to believe.
